notes: Curated interview questions, tagged against a CLOSED competency vocabulary. The vocabulary is closed for the same reason rubric_criteria is validated at load: a planner that may invent a competency name produces tags the bank can never match, and the failure is silent. Warmup and closing questions are deliberately absent -- they are structural, identical in every plan, and carry no competency. A question carries BOTH a source (where the text came from, immutable) and a status (whether it may be asked). Generation writes source=generated status=proposed; approval flips the status and never the source, because FR-2 requires a generated question to stay marked as one. `phase_affinity` says which phase of the plan a competency belongs to. It is data rather than logic because the mapping is a judgement someone should be able to read and disagree with, and because the design phase is not scored -- putting a competency there decides that it will be described rather than graded.

competencies.incident_response: diagnosing and resolving production failures, and what changed afterwards
competencies.performance: finding and fixing a scalability or latency problem, with measurement
competencies.data_modelling: schema and data-model change, especially against live data
competencies.system_design: designing a component or service against stated constraints
competencies.testing_quality: deciding something is correct and ready, and how that is known
competencies.collaboration: working through disagreement, feedback and shared decisions
competencies.ownership: supporting what they built after it shipped
competencies.learning: getting productive in an unfamiliar system quickly
competencies.technical_judgement: choosing between options and revisiting the choice later

questions.text: Describe a production incident you were responsible for resolving.
Tell me about a time you found the cause of something only after your first explanation turned out to be wrong.
Describe a failure that reached users before anyone on the team noticed it.
Walk me through a performance or scalability problem you've hit. What did you measure, and what did you change?
Tell me about a time you made something faster and could show by how much.
Describe a time you decided a performance problem was not worth fixing.
Tell me about a schema or data-model change you've made to a system that was already live.
Describe a data model you inherited and had to work against rather than change.
Tell me about a migration or backfill you ran, and how you knew it had worked.
Walk me through how you'd design a rate limiter for a public API. Take a minute first if you want.
How would you design a service that has to keep working when the database it depends on is unavailable? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose you had to move a nightly batch job to run continuously instead. How would you approach it? Take a minute first if you want.
Describe how you decide a change is ready to ship. Use a recent example.
Tell me about a bug that your tests should have caught and didn't.
Describe a time you shipped something deliberately without full test coverage.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision on your team.
Tell me about a time you gave difficult feedback to a colleague.
Describe a decision your team made that you disagreed with and went along with anyway.
Describe how you've handled being on-call, or supporting something you built.
Tell me about something you shipped that didn't work out the way you expected.
Tell me about a piece of work you finished that nobody asked you to do.
Tell me about a time you had to learn an unfamiliar codebase quickly.
Describe something technical you had to learn recently because the work required it.
Tell me about a technical decision you made that you'd make differently now.
Describe a time you chose the slower, more careful approach and had to justify it.
Tell me about a time you removed something rather than adding to it.
Describe a time you helped someone else get unstuck on work that wasn't yours.
Tell me about a review comment you left that changed how someone worked.
